opus-5.5.text:
I'm cautiously optimistic, but I think it's important to be honest about where the difficulty lies. SAT and SMT solvers have historically been very hard to accelerate on GPUs because the core algorithms, things like conflict-driven clause learning, are deeply sequential and irregular. You're chasing pointers through clause databases, doing unit propagation that branches unpredictably, and learning clauses on the fly. That's almost the opposite of the dense, regular, data-parallel workloads that GPUs are built for. So for years the honest answer was that people tried, and the speedups were modest or didn't hold up against a well-tuned CPU solver.

That said, I think the picture is shifting in a few interesting ways. First, there's a lot of work on reformulating parts of the reasoning problem so they map better onto parallel hardware: things like local search methods, certain preprocessing and simplification steps, and algebraic or matrix-based encodings of problems that look more like linear algebra. Second, portfolio and distributed approaches, where you run many diverse solver configurations or partition the search space across many cores, have worked really well in the cloud, and some of those ideas may carry over to accelerators. And third, there's the interplay with machine learning. If you're using learned models to guide heuristics, like which variable to branch on or which lemma to try, then the neural part runs naturally on GPUs, even if the symbolic core stays on CPUs.

So my view is that the near-term win probably isn't "port the whole solver to a GPU." It's hybrid architectures, where the symbolic reasoning that has to be sound and exact stays where it runs best, and the parts that are statistical, parallel, or search-guidance-oriented get pushed onto the accelerators. And at the end of the day, whatever hardware is producing the answer, you still want a checkable proof, something you can verify independently, because that's really the value proposition of automated reasoning. Speed is great, but trust is the thing we're actually selling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is: it's harder than people assume, but there's real progress and I'm more optimistic than I was five years ago.

The core issue is that the classic solvers — SAT, SMT, the things we build on at Amazon for tools like Zelkova and the automated reasoning checks in Bedrock — are fundamentally search problems with a lot of irregular, data-dependent control flow. CDCL, the conflict-driven clause learning algorithm at the heart of modern SAT, is almost adversarial to GPUs. You're doing unit propagation through a sparse structure, the memory accesses are all over the place, and the key insight is that the algorithm makes decisions sequentially and learns from conflicts. Branch divergence kills you. So the naive thing — "let's just port MiniSat to CUDA" — people tried that in the late 2000s and it didn't really go anywhere.

That said, I'd point to a few places where I think the picture is changing.

First, there are sub-problems inside the solvers that are embarrassingly parallel. Preprocessing and inprocessing — things like bounded variable elimination, subsumption checks, probing — those are much more amenable. And there's been nice work on doing propagation in a more data-parallel style, using something closer to a matrix-vector formulation of the clause database. It doesn't replace CDCL, but it can be a useful co-processor.

Second, and I think this is the more interesting direction, is the local search and stochastic side. Algorithms in the WalkSAT family, or the newer approaches that look a bit like simulated annealing or belief propagation, map really nicely onto GPUs because you're doing lots of independent or loosely coupled evaluations. For certain problem classes — random instances, some optimization-flavored problems, MaxSAT-ish things — you can get genuine speedups. The trouble is that for the industrial, structured instances we care about in verification, those methods have historically been weaker. So you end up with portfolio approaches: run the GPU-based local search alongside the CPU-based CDCL and take whichever finishes first.

Third — and this is where I spend a lot of my time thinking — is the interaction with machine learning. Once you're training neural networks to guide heuristics, whether that's variable selection, restart policies, or which lemmas to keep, the GPU is doing something it's genuinely good at. The reasoning engine stays on the CPU, but the "intuition" layer lives on the accelerator. I think that's the realistic near-term architecture: hybrid, with the symbolic core remaining sequential and exact, and the learned components off to the side providing guidance.

There's also a hardware angle. Some of the newer accelerators aren't quite GPUs — they're more like custom dataflow or annealing-style hardware — and a handful of groups are looking at whether you can express propagation or resolution directly in those terms. I'm cautious there. A lot of those claims about "solving SAT on a quantum annealer" or whatever don't hold up on the instances that matter.

So, if you're asking me to make a prediction: I don't think we'll see a drop-in GPU replacement for the core of a modern SMT solver in the near future. The sequential, learning-from-conflicts nature is a feature, not a bug — that's why these things scale to millions of variables at all. But I do think the overall pipeline is getting more parallel at the edges, and the ML-guided pieces are going to push more of the work onto accelerators. For us, where the goal is giving customers a mathematical proof that their access policies or their network configurations do what they think, correctness is non-negotiable. So whatever we do on the GPU side has to be something we can check — a heuristic that makes the proof search faster is great, but the proof itself still has to come out of the exact engine.

r002.rationale: It describes propagation using a matrix-vector formulation of the clause database as a data-parallel approach that can make GPU acceleration useful.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s real potential, but it’s not as straightforward as taking an existing solver and running it on a GPU. The question is whether you can organize the reasoning so that you have lots of similar operations happening in parallel. Solvers often involve irregular search, branching, and dependencies between steps, which makes that challenging.

So I’m optimistic, but I’d distinguish accelerating particular parts of a solver from accelerating the whole thing. We may need to rethink the algorithms around the hardware, rather than simply port what we already have. The interesting test is whether that gives us an end-to-end improvement on the problems we actually want to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an opportunity there, but it’s not as straightforward as taking an existing solver and running it on a GPU. A lot of automated reasoning involves irregular search: you’re branching, learning things, and changing what you do next. That’s a different workload from the dense numerical operations where GPUs have been so successful.

The interesting question is whether we can reformulate parts of the reasoning process to expose enough parallelism to make acceleration worthwhile. You might accelerate particular operations, or explore many candidate solutions in parallel, while keeping other parts on the CPU. I’m optimistic about that, but I’d distinguish the potential from a demonstrated, end-to-end improvement. Ultimately, we need to show that it helps solve the problems people actually care about.
